rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Viruses are acellular, obligate intracellular parasites that contain either DNA or RNA enclosed in a protein capsid (and sometimes a lipid envelope). They cannot replicate outside a host cell and hijack host machinery. The T4 bacteriophage lytic cycle (adsorption, injection, replication, assembly, release) is the NEB model.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Virus = Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) + Capsid (protein) [+ Envelope (lipid + glycoprotein)]
Lytic cycle: Adsorption → Penetration (injection) → Biosynthesis → Assembly → Release
Lysogenic cycle: Prophage integration → Replication with host → Induction → Lytic cycle

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Viruses are NOT living organisms: they lack metabolism, cannot reproduce outside a host, and are not made of cells.  ·  A virus has EITHER DNA or RNA, never both (with rare exceptions like some retroviruses that convert RNA to DNA).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a detailed T4 phage diagram and the 5-step lytic cycle.  ·  The "are viruses alive?" debate is a favourite exam discussion; present both arguments.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: T4 bacteriophage — DNA virus, infects E. coli; lytic cycle model.  ·  Influenza virus — RNA virus, causes seasonal flu.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Bacteriophages infect BACTERIA; animal viruses infect animals; plant viruses infect plants.  ·  The capsid is protein; the core is nucleic acid; the envelope (if present) is lipid + glycoproteins from the host membrane.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Label T4 phage  ·  Draw the lytic cycle (5 steps)

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Virus = V-O-I (Very small, Obligate, Infectious).  ·  T4 phage = icosahedral head + tail = "phage = eater of bacteria".

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Why are viruses called "acellular"?  ·  Describe the structure of a T4 bacteriophage with a labelled diagram.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Draw and label a T4 bacteriophage — very common.  ·  Describe the lytic life cycle in 5 steps.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Acellular nature  ·  Capsid and envelope  ·  DNA vs RNA viruses  ·  T4 phage structure

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Viruses are acellular, obligate intracellular parasites.  ·  Structure: nucleic acid + capsid (+ envelope in some).  ·  DNA or RNA (not both); capsomeres form the capsid.  ·  Bacteriophage: icosahedral head + tail + baseplate + tail fibers.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The largest virus (Pithovirus) is ~1.2 µm in diameter — visible only under a light microscope.  ·  Smallpox was the first human disease eradicated by vaccination (1980).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Explain the lytic life cycle of a bacteriophage (5 steps).  ·  Differentiate a DNA virus from an RNA virus.  ·  What is the significance of the viral envelope?

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Differentiate DNA and RNA viruses.  ·  Explain why viruses are not living organisms.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) — retrovirus, causes AIDS.  ·  SARS-CoV-2 — RNA virus, causes COVID-19.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A virus contains: → B  ·  The T4 bacteriophage infects: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Viruses: acellular, obligate intracellular parasites; not classified in any kingdom; consist of a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) + protein coat (capsid); some have a lipid envelope.  ·  Structure: capsomeres (protein subunits of capsid); bacteriophages have a head (icosahedral) + tail; animal viruses may have an envelope with glycoprotein spikes.  ·  Types by nucleic acid: DNA viruses (e.g., T4 phage, smallpox) and RNA viruses (e.g., influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Gene therapy applications  ·  Lytic cycle: 5 steps, destroys host; Lysogenic: integrates, delays lysis.  ·  Not living: no metabolism, no independent reproduction.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Importance: cause many diseases; used in gene therapy and research.  ·  Lytic cycle destroys the host cell; lysogenic cycle integrates viral DNA into the host genome (prophage) without immediate lysis.  ·  Viruses are NOT visible under a light microscope; they require an electron microscope (~20–300 nm size).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: DNA vs RNA viruses: know the key difference and one example of each.  ·  Mention the significance of the viral envelope (immune evasion, cell entry).  ·  Memorise the T4 phage structure (head, tail, baseplate, fibers).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Learn the 5 steps of the lytic cycle.  ·  Differentiate DNA and RNA viruses with examples.  ·  Explain why viruses are not considered living.
